nameStory: The common poppy earned its "corn poppy" and "field poppy" names because it thrived as a weed in grain fields, where "corn" was the old European term for any cereal crop like wheat or barley. It's also called the Flanders poppy because it famously grew in the war-torn fields of Belgium during World War I, inspiring the poem "In Flanders Fields" and becoming a symbol of remembrance.
description: The common poppy is a cheerful annual wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with delicate, papery red petals that seem to glow in sunlight. Each flower has four silky petals that look almost tissue-thin, surrounding a dark center with prominent black stamens. The plants have deeply lobed, feathery leaves and tend to grow in patches where the soil has been disturbed. Though originally from Europe and North Africa, these hardy flowers have made themselves at home in New England's fields and roadsides.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Four brilliant red, papery-thin petals that feel like silk and often have a dark blotch at the base; petals are so delicate they seem translucent when backlit by the sun

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery leaves that feel slightly rough and hairy to the touch, with narrow segments that give them a lacy appearance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, smooth seed pods about the size of a marble with a flat top that opens like a salt shaker, releasing tiny dark seeds when ripe

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems that feel hollow and release a milky white sap when broken, often growing in clusters in disturbed soil areas

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Flower buds hang downward like tiny green teardrops covered in coarse hairs, then flip upright just before the petals unfurl

habitat: Look for common poppies in disturbed soils like old farm fields, roadsides, vacant lots, and construction sites throughout New England's lowlands and valleys. They particularly love areas where the ground has been recently turned over, as the seeds need full sunlight to germinate. You'll often find them mixed with other weedy wildflowers in sunny, open spaces with poor to average soil.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate early and young plants develop their characteristic feathery leaves, forming low rosettes that are easy to overlook among other emerging weeds.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with brilliant red flowers opening in the morning sun, though individual flowers last only a day or two before the petals drop.
seasonality.fall: Plants set seed in their distinctive round capsules and die back, but seeds scatter and can remain dormant in soil for many years until conditions are right.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain, but countless seeds lie waiting in the soil, ready to sprout when spring brings warmth and soil disturbance.

funFact: A single common poppy plant can produce over 17,000 seeds, and these seeds can remain viable in the soil for over 80 years, waiting for the perfect moment when soil disturbance brings them back to the surface and sunlight triggers their germination!
confusionNotes: Garden varieties of Oriental poppies are much larger with more orange-red petals, while other red wildflowers like field chickweed have many more than four petals. Remember: four silky petals plus that distinctive milky sap means common poppy.
contextualKnowledge: While this species shares a genus with the opium poppy, the common poppy contains no narcotic compounds and is completely legal to grow. The red poppy's association with remembrance comes from its habit of blooming in disturbed soil, including the battlefields of World War I where it grew among the graves of fallen soldiers.
compareHints: Common poppy is much smaller and more delicate than Oriental poppy, with thinner petals and smaller flowers. Unlike opium poppy, which has smooth, waxy leaves that clasp the stem, common poppy has deeply divided, hairy leaves. The long-headed poppy has similar flowers but elongated seed pods rather than the round "pepper shaker" pods of common poppy.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the common red poppy with its bright scarlet petals and hairy stems, opium poppies have that distinctive blue-green, waxy appearance and much larger flowers in various colors.

Unlike its annual cousins like corn poppy (which has smaller, more delicate flowers and stays visible all season), Oriental poppy is a robust perennial with much larger flowers and hairy, substantial foliage.
Long-headed poppy is most easily distinguished from corn poppy (Papaver rhoeas) by its elongated seed capsules versus corn poppy's round ones.
Unlike the bright red Common Poppy or the large, vivid Oriental Poppy, Atlas Poppy has distinctly pale orange flowers that are much more subtle.
